name: First Battle of the Marne
info: French and British armies under Joffre counter-attacked the German right wing between Paris and Verdun in September 1914, forced the Germans to retreat to the Aisne and ended the German plan for a quick victory in the west.

facts.date: 5 to 12 September 1914; the German retreat is also dated 9 to 13 September
facts.place: Between Paris and Verdun along the Marne valley, northern France, on a west-to-east front of 230 km; the most severe fighting was in the western half
facts.sides: France and the British Expeditionary Force under Joseph Joffre and John French, with 980,000 French and 100,000 British soldiers between Paris and Verdun on the eve of battle; Germany under Helmuth von Moltke, whose armies there numbered 750,000
facts.outcome: The German 1st and 2nd Armies were at risk of encirclement and, with the other German armies, retreated to the Aisne, ending the German attempt to defeat France quickly; the armies then dug in on the Aisne.

t: The Franco-British counter-attack of September 1914 halted the German advance on Paris and ended the Schlieffen Plan, the German plan to defeat France in about six weeks.

A gap of 50 km opened between the German 1st and 2nd Armies, and the French 5th Army and the British Expeditionary Force advanced into it, while communications between the German armies and Moltke's headquarters were poor.

Casualty estimates differ widely: about 250,000 French, 12,733 British and 298,000 Germans in one estimate, and about 300,000 for all sides in another that questions whether the battle can be separated from its surroundings.
dyk: Joseph Gallieni commandeered about 600 Paris taxicabs on the night of 7 to 8 September to carry soldiers to the front; the meters ran, and the French treasury paid a fare of 70,012 francs.
ev: German armies win most of the battles of the opening campaign and overrun much of Belgium and northern France
Joffre abandons Plan XVII and the Great Retreat of the French and British begins
Moltke changes the German plan, and Kluck's 1st Army turns south-east and crosses the Marne
Joffre halts the retreat and orders a counter-offensive
The 6th Army meets the German IV Reserve Corps at the Ourcq, and the 5th Army and the BEF advance into the gap between the 1st and 2nd Armies
Hentsch's staff tour leads to a general German retreat to the Aisne
Moltke is replaced by Falkenhayn, and the First Battle of the Aisne begins
Both sides try to turn each other's northern flank in the Race to the Sea

sections.background:
Germany declared war on France on 3 August 1914, and both sides expected a short war. Germany faced a war on two fronts, against Russia in the east and against France and Britain in the west. Under the Schlieffen Plan, as revised by Helmuth von Moltke, the German armies were to sweep through Belgium and into France, capture Paris and envelop and destroy the French army east of the city within about six weeks, and then turn on Russia. The violation of Belgian neutrality brought the United Kingdom into the war, and Britain sent the British Expeditionary Force (BEF) to France. France's chief aim was to recover Alsace-Lorraine, lost to Germany in 1870, and its Plan XVII expected the main German force in the east.

August brought bloody battles that the Germans nearly all won. Charles Lanrezac and the retired general Joseph Gallieni warned Joffre that the main German effort lay in the north-west, and on 24 August Joffre acknowledged that his left flank was at risk. He abandoned Plan XVII, and the French 3rd, 4th and 5th Armies and the BEF began a retreat of 300 km, mostly walking rather than fighting. Joffre created the 6th Army to defend Paris and the 9th Army under Ferdinand Foch, and moved troops by rail from his eastern armies.

The pursuing Germans had outrun their supplies. Kluck's 1st Army was 140 km beyond its railhead, and sixty per cent of its motor transport had broken down. Moltke had also reduced the force in France by 200,000 or more men, sending two corps east against the Russians and two to besiege Antwerp and Maubeuge.
sections.forces:
Germany had seven armies on the western front, and three on its right flank were most involved at the Marne: the 1st Army under Alexander von Kluck, which began the war with 320,000 men, the 2nd under Karl von Bülow with 260,000, and the 3rd under Max von Hausen with 180,000. These numbers had fallen by September. The 1st and 2nd Armies had 580,000 soldiers on 1 August and 372,000 at the battle. On the French side the 4th Army under Fernand de Langle de Cary, the 5th Army, the new 6th Army under Michel-Joseph Maunoury and Foch's 9th Army were most involved. Joffre dismissed Lanrezac on 3 September and replaced him with Louis Franchet d'Espèrey. The BEF, under John French, numbered 130,000 at the start of the war.

On the eve of battle the allied forces between Paris and Verdun numbered 980,000 French and 100,000 British soldiers, against 750,000 Germans. The Germans had 3,300 guns to 3,000.

The commanders differed. Moltke stayed at his headquarters in Luxembourg and gave his army commanders wide latitude. Joffre visited his armies often and dismissed more than 30 French generals. John French, shaken by the early British casualties, had been reluctant to engage the Germans. On 2 September Moltke ordered Paris bypassed on the north and made Bülow's army the main striking force, with Kluck to follow in echelon. Kluck instead turned south-east, crossed the Marne on 3 September and pursued the French 5th Army, unaware of the new 6th Army guarding Paris on his right.
sections.course:
On 4 September Joffre ordered the retreat halted and a counter-offensive to begin on 6 September. On 5 September part of Maunoury's 6th Army, probing north-east of Paris near the Ourcq, met the German IV Reserve Corps of 24,000 men under Hans von Gronau. Gronau attacked and held the French for 24 hours, which warned Kluck, who turned his army west and marched 130 km in two days to face the 6th Army. On the night of 7 to 8 September Gallieni sent soldiers to the front by rail, truck and about 600 Paris taxis. On 9 September Kluck's general von Quast broke through the 6th Army's defences, and the road to Paris, 50 km away, was open.

Meanwhile Bülow's depleted 2nd Army was attacked by the French 5th Army, and Hausen assaulted Foch's 9th Army at night on 8 September, pushing it back 13 km before his attack bogged down. Kluck's turn had opened a 50 km gap between his army and Bülow's, which French aerial reconnaissance discovered. The BEF and the 5th Army advanced into it, though the British moved slowly, advancing only 40 km in three days against a force they outnumbered ten to one.

On 8 September Moltke's staff officer Richard Hentsch visited the armies. At Bülow's headquarters he agreed that a general retreat would be necessary if the French and British crossed the Marne, and on 9 September he told Kluck's staff that a retreat was necessary. Bülow and Kluck withdrew, and on 11 September Moltke ordered the other armies back to the Aisne.
sections.aftermath:
The German armies retreated about 65 km to the north of the Aisne, where they dug in on the heights. The Franco-British pursuit averaged only 19 km a day. The Germans lost 11,717 prisoners, 30 field guns and 100 machine guns to the French and 3,500 prisoners to the British. Moltke wrote to his wife on the night of 9 September that things had not gone well. On 14 September he was told to resign for ill health, and Erich von Falkenhayn replaced him. The retreat ended the German hope of pushing the French beyond the Verdun-Marne-Paris line and winning a quick victory.

Casualties are hard to separate from those of the other battles of August and September. One estimate gives about 250,000 French, 12,733 British and 298,000 German casualties. Herwig estimated about 300,000 for all sides, with 67,700 for the five German armies, about 85,000 French and 1,701 British. Nelipovich estimated German losses at 10,602 killed, 16,815 missing and 47,432 wounded, and Entente losses at about 268,500.

The French 6th Army and the BEF advanced for four days against rearguards, but could not catch the Germans, and frontal attacks on the Aisne on 15 and 16 September were repulsed. Both sides then tried to turn each other's northern flank in the Race to the Sea, which led to the First Battle of Ypres and to trench warfare along a front that stayed nearly stable for four years.
sections.sources:
Historians reconstruct the battle from the memoirs and orders of its commanders and from the armies' official histories. Gallieni and Joffre wrote memoirs, and Moltke wrote to his wife on the night of 9 September. French casualty figures come from the French official history, Les armées françaises dans la grande guerre, German figures from the Sanitätsberichte and British figures from the British Official History. Later historians include John Keegan, Holger Herwig, Barbara Tuchman, Strachan and Ian Sumner.

Several points are disputed. Moltke is said to have told the Kaiser, "Your Majesty, we have lost the war", but whether he said so is not known. Moltke's instructions to Hentsch were verbal and not written, so what authority Hentsch held to order a retreat is a matter of what the participants reported. Gallieni wrote that some had exaggerated the importance of the taxis, and Strachan and Herwig regard their military effect as slight, though the effect on French morale is undeniable. Meyer wrote that the battle was "settled by one side's decision not to fight".

The casualty figures are uncertain, since over two million men fought in the campaign and no exact official counts exist. Estimates of casualties along the Marne front for all armies are often c. 500,000 killed or wounded, against Herwig's 300,000, and Herwig himself questioned whether isolating the battle was justified.
sections.legacy:
The German retreat marked the end of the Schlieffen Plan. Germany had hoped to win quickly in the west, and the failure meant a long war against France, Britain and Russia, whose combined resources were far greater than its own. Richard Brooks wrote that Joffre, by frustrating the plan, had won the decisive battle of the war and perhaps of the century. Herwig called it the most important land battle of the twentieth century, and John J. Tierney Jr argued that it was the most important battle in history. It was also one of the first battles in which reconnaissance aircraft played an important role, by finding the gap in the German lines.

Others judge it a partial success. John Terraine wrote that it never presented the traditional aspect of victory, yet called it the decisive battle of the war. Tuchman called it an incomplete victory, Doughty wrote that the opportunity for a decisive victory had slipped from Joffre's hands, and Ian Sumner called it a flawed victory. Joffre credited d'Espèrey with making it possible, and Kluck, according to Tuchman, put the German failure down to the French soldier's capacity to recover quickly.

In French memory it is the "miracle on the Marne" (miracle de la Marne). The Paris taxis, though militarily slight in the view of Strachan and Herwig, became the most storied event of the battle.

summary: From 5 to 12 September 1914 French and British armies counter-attacked the German right wing between Paris and Verdun, exploited a gap between two German armies and forced a retreat to the Aisne. The German plan for a quick victory failed, and the western front settled into trenches.
references: H. Herwig, The Marne, 1914: The Opening of World War I and the Battle that Changed the World (Random House, 2009)
I. Sumner, The First Battle of the Marne 1914: The French 'miracle' halts the Germans (Osprey, 2010)
R. B. Asprey, The First Battle of the Marne (Weidenfeld & Nicolson, 1962)
R. A. Doughty, Pyrrhic Victory: French Strategy and Operations in the Great War (Belknap Press, 2005)
S. Tyng, The Campaign of the Marne 1914 (Westholme Publishing, 2007)
B. Tuchman, The Guns of August (Constable, 1962)
notes: The article gives the German retreat as 9 to 12 September in the lead and 9 to 13 September in the aftermath; both are in facts.date. Its retreat distances also differ: 65 km (lead and Hentsch section) and up to 90 km (aftermath); I used 65 km. The Great Retreat is 250 km (lead) or 300 km (section); I used 300 km.

The article says the 6000 soldiers carried by rail, truck and taxi were critical, then that the taxis were insignificant; I gave the disputes without a verdict. The statement that Quast broke through on 9 September is followed by the retreat, and the article does not explain how the two fit.

Article gives casualties in three places (250,000 French / 12,733 British / 298,000 German in the lead; Herwig; Nelipovich; and c. 500,000 for all armies). The lead's British 12,733 (Sumner) conflicts with 1,701 (Herwig) and 13,000; I gave Herwig's 1,701 and the lead's figures. Herwig's 85,000 French is his assumption.

The French 5th Army is said to have massacred 450 Germans attempting to surrender; left out for length. Left out also: Joffre's 'honour of England' remark, Hausen's 11,000 casualties, the Kluck-Bülow rivalry, Tierney-style praise beyond the attributed verdicts, the Aisne and Race to the Sea operational detail.

The article's section on Kluck says Quast 'fought his way through' on the morning after 8 September; I wrote 9 September. The passage on Hentsch has him arriving at Kluck's HQ at 11:30 on 9 September.
The Herwig quotation about 'all-or-nothing throw of the dice' was left out. The sentence 'The French treasury paid the total fare of 70,012 francs' is used in dyk.
